awd_titl_txt: Doctoral Dissertation Research: Dimensions of Trust and Risk, and Their Effects on Civic Participation
awd_abstract_narration:
This research explores how different types of trust are related to people’s willingness to take risks, and tests whether the interplay between trust and risk taking is related to how people think about and participate in the civic system. While existing scholarship emphasizes the role of trust in shaping civic attitudes and behavior, research often overlooks how one’s willingness to take risks can vary across different aspects of life, and neglects how risk taking might affect the extent to which trust affects civic participation. By systematically investigating how trust and risk interact to shape civic attitudes and behavior, this project aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of civic engagement, for example, why individuals might trust the government but remain skeptical of the electoral process, or why people continue to participate in civic activities despite increasing distrust in civic elites and institutions over time. 

Leveraging original data collected during the November 2024 presidential election, this project examines the relationship between different types of trust and risk taking, hypothesizing that the extent to which people rely on trust may depend on how willing they are to take certain risks. Whereas individuals who are less willing to take certain risks may rely more on trust when deciding whether to vote or engage in other civic activities, those who are more willing to take certain risks may rely less on trust when deciding whether to participate. Combined with complementary experimental data, this project provides robust evidence on the roles of trust and risk taking in shaping civic attitudes and behavior. These data will also be used to develop a novel and validated measure of civic risk taking. Findings from this research help advance interdisciplinary scholarship while offering policymakers, scholars, and society guidance for mitigating deficits in trust, enhancing civic participation, and improving democratic health.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Major Goals: This project investigates how individual-level risk attitudes and political trust relate to each other and Americans' political participation. The central goals are to 1) establish the psychometric structure of political risk-taking, (2) examine how political risk-taking relates to electoral trust, and (3) identify causal pathways from risk attitudes and trust.

Major Activities: During this reporting period, I collected three original, nationally representative samples of US adults. I completed psychometric analysis of the conventional Domain-Specific Risk-Taking (DOSPERT) scale and developed an original, complementary political risk scale. Studies exploring the correlates and causal relationship between political risk and trust are underway. 

Significant Results: Preliminary findings indicate that political risk is related to, but distinct from, general risk-taking and risk-taking in other specific domains. I have also identified that political risk-taking is largely stable but may change in response to identifying with the winning/losing party in an election, and that the relationship between risk and winning/losing holds when controlling for other covariates (including other types of risk). 

Key Outcomes: Manuscript replicating the DOSPERT bifactor replication is in late-stage preparation for submission to a peer-reviewed journal. Chapter on the development and validation of political risk-taking has been reviewed by the dissertation committee. The last of my survey data is being collected in mid-May 2026 and two additional chapters are underway. 

Training and Professional Development: The co-PI has received additional training in skills necessary for this project (e.g., bifactor modeling, latent profile analysis, and Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition). Collaboration with PI Kyle L. Saunders has provided additional mentorship in large-scale survey design and computational methods.

Dissemination: Findings have been presented to political science and interdisciplinary audiences through conference participation. The DOSPERT replication manuscript is being prepared for peer review.

Products: Three original data sets, two completed dissertation chapters; two additional chapters underway.

Participants: Erin Fitz (co-PI), Doctoral Candidate (12 months); Kyle Saunders (PI), Faculty Advisor (12 months)

IMPACTS

Impacts to Primary Discipline: This project advances our understanding of how political risk-taking, trust, and the relationship between political risk-taking and trust, relate to Americans’ political attitudes and behavior.

Impacts to Other Disciplines: Findings also contribute to judgment and decision-making research by expanding upon conventional measures of risk. 

Impacts to Society Beyond Science and Technology: Understanding how risk-taking and trust jointly help to explain political attitudes and behavior has direct implications for electoral engagement and democratic representation.

Changes/Problems: Nothing to report.


Last Modified: 04/15/2026
Modified by: Erin B Fitz
